title: The Rendering Pipeline: DOM → CSSOM → Paint
objectives: Describe the stages from HTML source to composited pixels
Classify style changes as layout, paint or composite work
Use transform and opacity to keep animations off the layout path
Spot reflow and repaint hotspots in a Performance panel recording
body:
The browser does not paint your page in one step. It parses HTML into the **DOM**, parses CSS into the **CSSOM**, merges both into a render tree, computes **layout** (geometry), **paints** pixels into layers, and finally **composites** layers onto the screen. Each stage has a very different cost, and knowing which stage a change triggers is the first performance skill worth learning.

## The problem
A menu animation in your app stutters on cheap laptops, and every attempted fix — minifying CSS, swapping animation libraries — changes nothing. The team is guessing because nobody can name the pipeline stage that is slow.

## Constraints
- Layout (reflow) recomputes geometry and can cascade through the whole render tree, so it is the most expensive stage.
- Paint rasterizes pixels: it skips geometry work but still pays per-pixel cost.
- Compositing runs on the GPU and is by far the cheapest stage.
- Only `transform` and `opacity` changes are guaranteed to skip layout *and* paint.
- At 60 Hz the frame budget is about 16.7 ms; a slower stage means dropped frames.

## Options
Suppose a card slides into view. Three realistic implementation options:

```css
/* A: animate layout properties */
.card-a { transition: left 0.3s, width 0.3s; }   /* layout + paint every frame */

/* B: animate paint-only properties */
.card-b { transition: background 0.3s, color 0.3s; } /* paint, no layout */

/* C: animate composited properties */
.card-c { transition: transform 0.3s, opacity 0.3s; } /* composite only */
```

Option A re-runs layout every frame and can blow the frame budget on its own. Option B removes the layout step but still repaints. Option C promotes the element to its own layer and hands the animation to the compositor thread, so it keeps running smoothly even while the main thread is busy — the biggest win for the smallest code change.

## Tradeoffs
Compositor-only animation is not free: every promoted layer consumes GPU memory, and `will-change` forces layer creation even while idle. Layer explosion on low-memory devices can hurt more than the jank it fixes, so promotion is a scalpel, not a default for every element.

## Decision
Default to `transform` and `opacity` for anything that moves. Touch `width`, `top` or `margin` only when the design truly requires re-layout, and treat that as a measured cost, not a style choice. Reserve `will-change` for a handful of known-hot elements and remove it when the interaction ends.

## Measure it
In DevTools → Performance, record while the animation runs. Purple *Recalculate Style* and green *Layout* bars mean you are on the layout path; *Paint* bars mean repaint; neither means the compositor handled it. Always keep a before recording and compare it with the after recording under the same conditions.

## Best practices
- Animate `transform` and `opacity`; treat other animated properties as exceptions you can justify.
- Batch DOM reads before DOM writes so the engine never interleaves invalidation with queries.
- Keep DOM depth low in subtrees you update frequently.
- Use paint flashing and layer borders in DevTools to verify what the engine actually does.
- Record a baseline before optimizing and compare against it afterwards.

## Common mistakes
- Animating `height` or `top` and wondering why the flame chart is full of green Layout bars.
- Reading `offsetWidth` inside a loop that also writes styles, forcing synchronous reflow on every iteration.
- Sprinkling `will-change` across hundreds of elements and blowing the memory budget.
- Assuming declarative CSS is free — selectors are resolved during every style recalculation.
- Optimizing without measuring, so nobody can prove anything improved.

exercise.prompt: This classifier is supposed to label each CSS change with the pipeline stages it triggers, but it has a bug: every property is reported as paint. Fix stage() so width/height/top/left/margin/font-size report layout+paint, transform/opacity report composite only, and colors/backgrounds report paint. The list should render the corrected verdict for every change.
hints: Check the membership tables first: which list contains each property?
Test the layout and composite tables before falling back to paint.
transform and opacity are the only guaranteed composite-only properties.

questions.prompt: Which pair of property changes can typically be handled by the compositor without layout or paint?
questions.explanation: transform and opacity are the two properties the spec guarantees can be composited, so animating them skips both layout and paint.

questions.prompt: Reading offsetHeight immediately after writing styles in the same task causes what?
options: Nothing, the value comes from cache
A forced synchronous layout, serializing work the engine could have batched
An automatic promotion to its own compositor layer
The style recalculation to be skipped for that frame
questions.explanation: A layout-blocking read flushes all pending style and layout invalidations immediately, which is why interleaved reads and writes are called layout thrashing.
